Sounds like the main things entrepreneurs are worried about. Let me see if I can help.

1.) There are four main areas: Self investments, loans, handouts, and investors. Don't limit yourself to one, either. It can be any combination of the four. Self investment can take a long time depending on the type of business you're trying to start up, however you won't owe anyone anything once all is said and done. Loans are a bit risky but can come in handy. Just remember, if you don't end up succeeding with your start up, you'll still have to pay these off. Friends and Family can often come in handy to soften the blow financially by lending a few dollars here and there. Investors are the preferred method of most entrepreneurs, however you must have an air tight business plan and a great elevator pitch (1-minute presentation about your company). Watch Shark Tank (if possible) to understand some of the questions that will be thrown your way, you don't want to be left out to dry with no answer. The second part of that is your own option, there are plenty of Entrepreneurs that own multiple ventures and there are plenty that just stuck with one.

2.) There are programs like intuit or quickbooks to help you with the accounting, which is normally the hardest part for most people. Other than that, I would agree that you should read up on accounting, financing, marketing, management, etc.

3.) You will most likely be the sole worker for a time when you initially start up. I've heard stories about entrepreneurs working 14 hour days or 80 hour work weeks for a few months just to get their business off the ground. If you're truly invested in your idea and are passionate about the company, this shouldn't be as big of an issue as it seems, although it can suck. Once you gather enough revenues to be able to afford the expense of employees, a few things come into play, leadership being a big one. There are plenty of books out there on being an good leader, and there are plenty of different leadership styles. Read a few books, find which style works best for you, and hone it. Don't just manage your employees, motivate them. As for finding employees, friends from university can go a long way. You can also place ads on job sites and local papers. There will always be aspiring entrepreneurs such as myself who want to see start ups in action, and will do anything to help and learn. Also, hiring like-minded people can work as long as you wont be butting heads, so to speak. Hire employees whose skills will compliment each other, not mimic each other. The best teams are set up this way.

TL;DR: Self Investment, Loans, Handouts, and Investors. Study your subjects, and use helpful programs. You will most likely be the sole worker for a while but once you do get employees, find your leadership style, hone it, and lead your employees. Find people whose skills compliment each other.
